Children don’t. The young-at-heart don’t. 

As a matter of fact, we don’t. Even at this historic moment— 

the start of Centennial Year—we would rather look over the horizon 

than over our shoulder. Canada’s second century. What can we do with it? 

How can we make it even better, even more productive, than our first century? 

For our part, we’re intending to use even more imagination in everything we do. 
Lots more ingenuity. Many more scientific techniques that we haven t even 
dreamed of yet. And you-you’ll be shopping in ways you’ve never shopped before. 
Nicer shopping. More convenient shopping. Much more exciting shopping. 

1967. What a year to look forward to. What a century to look forward to. 

Happy Second Century!

Children and bears like honey. For 
this reason alone, the honeybee is a 
practical topic for intensive observation 
and investigation in an outdoor setting. 

Camp provides an ideal opportunity 
for the boy or girl to become better 
acquainted with the physical charac¬ 
teristics, the plants and animals of his 
or her environment. 

A Variety of Habitat 

A camp reconnaissance will reveal a 
variety of habitat — pond, marsh, 
swamp, grassland, forested, and refor¬ 
estation areas. In each, the topography, 
the sunlight, the soil, water, and air 
determine the plants that flourish. 
These provide food, beauty and shelter 
for the animals. 

Honeybees are found in a natural 
state, in hollow trees. By providing the 
beehive home, with removable Hoff¬ 
man frame interior, the beekeeper pro¬ 
vides a modern, efficient abode for the 
honeybees. In turn the bees provide 
much more honey for consumption in 
an accessible form in the beehive than 
is provided in the beetree. Also there 
will be a larger colony of bees for pol- 


HONEY BEES 

«it Camp 

by Sam G. Hambly, B.A. 

Directory Camp Allsaw 


filiation and fertilization of plants. ThL 
is a high form of conserv ation. 

To Begin 

To keep bees at camp, select an 
interested counsellor. For a twenty-fiv e 
dollar fee he can attend a one week 
short course on beekeeping at Guelph 
University, usually the first week of 
July. 

From the Ontario Honey Producers 
Co-Operative Ltd.. 5 Defries St., Tor¬ 
onto. Telephone 364-8266. one may 
purchase supplies. A good observation 
hive can be made by cutting out from 
the sides of a regular hive-body suitable 
hinged openings. These openings should 
be covered by glass on the inside to 
prevent the bees from escaping at other 
than the normal opening. Through 
O.H.P.C. Ltd. a 2-lb. package of bee< 
with a queen can be ordered for de¬ 
livery by mail to a city address during 
May. 

The package bees could be installed 
in the observation hive at camp during 
May. 

My camp observation hive is set up 
in a window, with an eastern exposure 
at a Toronto school in May. The bees 
have free access to the outdoors via a 
tunnel under or through the lower part 
of the window sash. 


78 


Canadian Camping 



In the resource room the pupils plant 
seedlings in flats and prepare soil for 
transplants. The small flower plants are 
set into individual containers filled with 
the prepared soil mixtures. The half 
pint milk cartons delivered to the 
school for underprivileged children, 
with drainage holes punched in the bot¬ 
tom are suitable for transplanting. 
Hence, the pupils provide plants to 
bloom and pasture the bees. At home 
in their backyards they observe the bees 
gathering nectar and pollen. At school 
through the windowed beehive, they 
observe the bees using the pollen and 
nectar from their own home gardens. 
The following winer it is sometimes 
feasible to have the pupils taste the 
comb honey made from the nectar and 
pollen of plants they have helped to 
propagate. 

In preparing the hive body for ob¬ 
servation, a full frame of drawn comb 
is placed in the central part of the 
chamber. Frames with a one-inch 
fringe of foundation are placed on 
either side of the full frame of drawn 
comb. This prevents the bees from 
hiding from view between the combs 
and thus provides for better observation. 

The Ontario Department of Agri¬ 
culture has for distribution a variety of 
informative booklets on all phases of 
beekeeping. These contain a wealth of 
ideas and instructions for the layman. 
The staff of the Department of Agri¬ 
culture, University of Guelph, is most 
generous in providing plans and discuss¬ 
ing problems. 

My observation hive is moved from 
the school windowledge in June to an 
outdoors location at camp. This should 
be a sheltered spot with good air drain¬ 
age and an easterly exposure to sun¬ 
light, shaded during the hot part of 
the day. 

The Observation Hive 

The observation hive provides a 
camp focal point for the observation 


of the development of the brood nest 
inside the glass windows. Here the 
campers will observe the bees building 
the hexagonal shaped cells for brood 
rearing and storing honey. They will 
marvel at the regularity, the beauty 
and accuracy of the honeybees’ handi¬ 
work. A worker may be observed pro¬ 
ducing a scale of fresh wax for con¬ 
struction from between two segments 
on the underside of the abdomen. The 
queen bee, attended by her retinue of 
servant helpers, may be seen depositing 
an egg on the bottom of a cell, pro¬ 
jecting at right angles from the base. 
Different stages of development in the 
life cycle—egg, larva, pupa and adult 
may be observed. 

Worker bees will be observed enter¬ 
ing the hive with their pollen baskets 
on their rear legs laden with pellets of 
pollen. Campers will see this highly 
nutritious, protein-packed food, stored 
in cells for future use in making bee- 
bread, a mixture of pollen and nectar. 

A thimble shaped queen cell may be 
discovered on the edge of a frame. 
Close observation may reveal the 
worker bees renovating an area of 
comb, tearing away the worker bee 
and honey ceils and constructing the 
larger and thimble shaped queen bee 
cell. 

A wide difference in the colour of 
pellets of pollen arouses the interest of 
observers. A pollen trap placed under 
the bottom super of the hive on a good 
day will collect a cup of pollen. A good 
camper activity is to have a group 
classify the pollen according to colour. 
Then close observation under a good 
microscope will reveal characteristic 
shapes of various species of pollen. 
From these forms the plants producing 
the pollen may be identified. 

And Afterwards . . . 

A few years ago I gave a sample of 
honey from the Highlands of Hali- 
burton to Dr. Maurice Smith as he was 


Toronto , Canada , April 1967 


79 


leaving on an apiculture research ex¬ 
pedition in France. I)r. Smith gave the 
sample to Dr. Louveaux, France, who 
in turn examined the traces of pollen 
it contained. Later, I received from 
Dr. Smith a report by the research 
worker on the variety of species of 
Canadian plants on which the honey 
bees pastured in collecting the nectar 
to produce the honey. 

For our camp in June a local’apiar- 
ist, Mr. Victor Peel, sets up on the 
camp site, a four colony apiary. Once 
each two week period, he comes to 
camp fetching with him his honey ex¬ 
tracting equipment. This is set up in 
the craft shop or dining hall. After 
collecting the honey laden frames from 
the beehives the campers in rotating 
groups, assist the apiarist in extracting 
the honey. As Victor uses the steam 
heated decapping knife to shear the 
caps ofT the honey filled cells. Mrs. 
Peel fills small paper cups with hot 
fresh honey cappings. These are eagerly 
consumed by curious campers. The 
taste makes a lasting impression. 

Containers are filled with the golden 
coloured fresh honey and set away for 
camp breakfast. Pound bottles arc 
filled and labelled with the Camp All¬ 
saw Apiary label and stored for sou¬ 
venirs for departing campers. 

From time to time the campers dis¬ 
cover swarms of honeybees in search of 
a new home. A year ago a very large 


swarm was discovered on the branch 
of an ash tree eight feet above ground 
level, at the end of the tent line. A 
spare hive body with some honev- 
odoured drawn comb was set on the 
ground nearby under the tree. With 
a step ladder and saw the branch sup¬ 
porting the swarm was removed and 
placed at the entrance of the hive. 
Within an hour the new colony had 
occupied their new dwelling and com¬ 
menced house cleaning, renovation, 
brood rearing and honey and pollen 
collecting. 

Honeybees must never be manipu¬ 
lated by an inexperienced operator in 
the presence of children. All steps 
using honeybees should be well prac¬ 
tised in private before children are 
exposed to the dangers of bee stings. 
Some campers are fatally allergic to 
bee sting. The utmost care must be 
practised at all times by an operator 
who has had considerable practice in 
private sessions. 

Properly handled with adequate pre¬ 
cautions honeybees can provide a 
fascinating interest at camp. The deli¬ 
cate flavours will arouse interest in the 
plants on which the honeybees pasture. 
Taste will supplement learning and 
understanding by sight. Invariably the 
camper through activity and first hand 
experience is motivated to explore 
further the phenomenal life of the 
honeybee. 


Sam G. Hambly has had considerable 
experience in using natural resources in 
an outdoor setting for instruction and 
recreation. He directed field trip excur¬ 
sions with Runnymcdc School pupils, 
Toronto from 1947-52 at “The Acres” 
in North York. In 1951 at the Ontario 
Agriculture College in Guelph, Mr. 
Hambly was the instructor in the De¬ 


partment of Education Workshop in 
Conservation. His services were utilized 
both in Europe and the United States. 
Currently he is with the Perth Avenue 
Junior School, Toronto, doing horti¬ 
cultural therapy, in the Guidance 
Workshop, and pupils' home gardens. 
Mr. Hambly founded Camp Allsaw in 
1962. 


80 


Canadian Camping 




/NTBRCUL JURAL 


CAMPING 


by H. K. Roessingh, M.A. 


For a number of reasons the owners 
of the Silvercrcek Ranch at Water 
Valley, Alberta responded with en¬ 
thusiasm to the suggestion that inter- 
cultural camping be made a centennial 
project lor the camping association. 
One of these reasons was that, as the 
only private camp in the Alberta Camp¬ 
ing Association the owners felt that 
they were possibly in a better position 
to introduce these camps and conse¬ 
quently had an obligation to undertake 
this. Another reason was that they, 
the Roessingh family, are immigrants 
themselves and so more sensitive to the 
implications of intercultural relations 
in Canada than many born Canadians. 

Pilot Projects 

Two camps were held in the summer 
of 1966; one sponsored by the Soropti- 
mist Club of Calgary, for children from 
10 to 12; the other an intercultural 
band camp sponsored by the Silver- 
creek Ranch for children from 13 to 
17. Both were considered pilot projects 
for more elaborate camps in 1967. Al¬ 
though many improvements will be 
needed in the programmes of these 
camps, each was considered an un¬ 
qualified success. 

The Soroptimist Club camp for 
youngsters from 10 to 12, was attended 
by a group of 14 Eskimos, Metis In¬ 
dians and white children from Aklavik 
and Inuvik in the N.W.T. in addition 
to a number of children from Indian 
Reserves in Alberta and others of a 
wide variety of cultural and ethnic 
backgrounds. Here success came almost 
too easily. How can you fail to keep 
a group of naturally cheerful children 
happy, if almost every thing they do 


and see is new to them? On arrival 
they crawl on the street to inspect the 
pavement that they never have seen 
before. On their first day their dearest 
wish is to see a cow and a horse and 
other farm animals. They can laugh 
with the others at themselves when 
one of them answers the question: “Do 
you speak Eskimo language?” with the 
shy response: “I don't speak any 
foreign languages.” 

With very few exceptions there was 
no sign of discrimination or prejudice 
and after the first few days the group 
mixed extremely well; there is litle 
doubt that everyone had a good time 
and wants to come back next summer. 
But if I were asked whether we 
achieved a lasting effect in intercultural 
relations, I would honestly have to say 
that I really don't know. The children 
were so eager to please us, that they 
answered any questions with the an¬ 
swers they thought we would like to 
have; they were too young and too 
shy to come forth with any deep 
thoughts on their relations to children 
from other races at the camp and to 
make comparisons with the situation 
in their daily life. For the 1967 camp 
our efforts will have to be concentrated 
on programming and evaluation. 

At the Intercultural Band Gamp, 
results in terms of improved intercul- 
tural understanding was more easily 
assessed. The main groups at the 
camp were English speaking children 
from Alberta and the N.W.T. and 
French speaking youngsters from Que¬ 
bec. The whole camp had one com¬ 
mon objective: to work together to- 


Tor onto, Canada , April 1967 


81 


wards a good result in music, their 
common interest. The cultural back¬ 
ground of the two main groups was 
aptly expressed in the programme 
played by the band, which included 
both French and Western pieces. In 
addition to five hours a day band prac¬ 
tice, the children went through an 
extensive programme of horseback rid¬ 
ing and other recreational activities as 
well as formal and informal discussions 
on a wide variety of subjects. The 
frankness in the discussions and the 
degree to which the language barrier 
was overcome surpassed our wildest 
expectations. 

Carry Over 

The delegates from Quebec were so 
pleased with the results of the camp, 
that not only have they announced 
that they will return with a larger 
delegation for our 1967 intercultural 
band camp, but also have invited a 
similar group from Western Canada 
to participate in a band camp at As¬ 
bestos, Quebec, which incidentally, 
again because the Silvercreek Ranch 
camp was such a success, will be the 
first resident band camp for both boys 
and girls in Quebec. 

Elaborate reports have been prepared 
on both the above camps. Details of 
the experiment and our plans for the 
future cannot be elaborated upon here, 
but the summer of 1966 proved to the 


complete satisfaction of the directors 
of the Silvercreek Ranch and to many 
of their guests that a camp provides 
the ideal setting for an intercultural 
experience. We have had an oppor¬ 
tunity to compare the camping experi¬ 
ment with other types of intercultural 
exchange; we have discussed the pro’s 
and con’s with participants in these 
programmes and have not found any 
othcr type of programme in which 
there was such a unanimous conviction 
that the experience was not only verv 
pleasant and instructive, but also 
achieved the purpose of intercultural 
understanding to very high degree. A 
parents’ committee has been formed in 
Alberta to assist the camp directors of 
the Silvercreek Ranch in the planning 
and promoting of future intercultural 
camps and to further study the possi¬ 
bilities of this project. 

We have only scratched the surface 
of the latent possibilities in this aspect 
of camping; we hope that many of our 
friends and colleagues in the camping- 
movement will show an interest and 
call on us to give them the benefit of 
our experience or let us have the bene¬ 
fit of similar experiences elsewhere. 
Surely the forthcoming seminar in 
Harrison Hotsprings, B.C. will bring 
together a core of people who can work 
together in programmes and ideas for 
intercultural camping.

Reading “Hank” Roessingh 3 s dossier made us wish 
we could share the whole thing with our readers — 
perhaps we will sometime. But for the moment here are 
a few facts. Mr. Roessingh was born in Holland, studied 
geology there and in Sweden and took his M.A. For six 
years he worked with an oil company in Sumatra, 
Indonesia where he got his first experience in round the 
year camping. He, his wife and their four children came 
to Canada in 1954 and a fifth child was born here. Since 
I960, Mr. Roessingh has been Honorary Vice Consul for 
the Netherlands in Calgary. The Roessinghs live at Silver 
Creek Ranch, Water Valley, Alberta. Mrs. Roessingh was 
a former president of the Alberta Comping Association.

Canadian Camping 



ON CHOOSING A SAILBOAT 

FOR CAMP 

by Norm McKee, 

Aquatic Director for the University of Waterloo and 
Director of the Kitchener Lions Youth Camp 


To begin with no amount of infor¬ 
mation that could be put into an article 
such as this will ever replace the 
advice of an experienced sailor. An 
experienced sailor will be able to give 
you specific advice tailored to your 
particular situation. 

A Few Points 

However, there are a few points, if 
kept in mind when purchasing a sail¬ 
boat, that may save you some later 
headaches. Two major factors will 
have an immediate bearing on what 
type of boat you will buy, economics 
and where you intend to sail. 

Let us first look at economics: the 
average price for a good “class” sail¬ 
boat will be approximately $70 per 
foot for a 16 ft sailboat; for every foot 
less deduct $5 (i.e., 8 ft. sailboat would 
cost $30 per foot). You would natur¬ 
ally be able to save a great deal if you 
buy kits and build your own boats. 
You will be able to buy sailboats for 
less, but these are usually not class 
boats. This may not prove to be a 
problem until you come to sell, re¬ 
place or repair your boat. The non¬ 
class boat is hard to sell. Often that 
particular type becomes obsolete and 
it gets progressively harder to get parts 
or repairs. So it is worth spending a 
little more initially to buy a class boat. 
The resale value alone will prove the 
initial investment worthwhile. Often 
the best time to buy is at the end of 
the sailing season. 


Class Boat 

Boats that are specially built to con¬ 
form to a certain formula and design, 
their features being similar to others in 
that particular class. Where you in¬ 
tend to sail your boat will have a great 
deal to do with the type of boat you 
will buy. II you are on a small inland 
lake where the wind seldom becomes 
very strong, a boat with a fibreglass 
hull (which is normally the lightest 
type of hull) and a fairly large sail area 
will be most suitable. Contrast this to 
a boat required for operation on large 
lakes such as the great lakes. Here a 
boat with fairly heavy hull and small 
sail area will prove to be more suitable 
for the average type camp. 

Other factors which will have to be 
taken into consideration, are things like 
maintenance, size of camp, type of 
programme, and staff availability. 

Maintenance 

In order to reduce the problems of 
maintenance it would be wise to con¬ 
sider these factors. The hull should be 
good quality fibreglass. The mast and 
boom should be aluminum. The stand¬ 
ing rigging should be either stainless 
steel or nylon. The running rigging 
should be nylon. The sails should be 
dacron. The hardware should be brass 
bronze or preferably stainless steel. A 
sailboat with all these features will be 
almost maintenance free and will stand 
up to camp usage much better. 


Toronto, Canada , April 1967 


83 


Size of Camp 

The size of the camp will dictate the 
size of boat. Generally:—an 8 ft. to 10 
ft. boat will take 1 adult or two small 
campers; a 10 ft. to 12 ft. boat can 
take 2 adults or 3 small campers; a 12 
ft. to 14 ft. boat will take 1 adult and 

3 to 4 small campers; and a 14 ft. to 
16 ft. will take 3 adults, or 1 adult and 

4 campers. Over 16 ft. means you are 
usually into some type of specialty 
programme such as tripping or cruis¬ 
ing. With these figures it is possible 
to work out, roughly, how many boats 
are needed. For example a camp that 
has cabin groupings of 8 to 10 would 
need 2 or 3, 12 ft. to 14 ft. boats, or 5, 
8 ft. boats. 

Type of Programme 

Another factor which will affect your 
decision will be the type of programme 
you intend operating. Is sailing a 
specialty or fill in type of programme? 
Will it have beginner or advanced or 
both elements? If it is a specialty of the 
camp, a class boat is a must preferably 
in the 14 ft. to 16 ft. class. You should 
also endeavour to have three boats of 
the same class as this way you can 
teach effective racing techniques. If it 
is purely an introductory type of an 
activity, the heavier , hull boat would 
be more suitable. Normally the heavier 
the hull the more stable the boat will 
be. If you have both beginner and ad¬ 
vanced sailors, two smaller heavier 
hulled boat for beginners and the 
lighter, larger hulled boat for the more 
advanced would be required. 

Staff* Availability 

One should be careful when selecting 
staff for a sailing programme; he should 
be as much a specialist as the craft 
director. No matter how careful you 
have been in selecting your boat the 
proper staff can make or break your 
programme. Even the best boats it 
poorly tuned can be a headache. A 


good sailing staff can get the best out 
of your boats. 

At no time in this article have I 
attempted to sell one boat in prefer¬ 
ence to another. This has been delib¬ 
erate for I know of no one class boat, 
of a particular size that is popular in 
all areas of Canada. There are many 
good class boats of varying sizes avail¬ 
able almost anywhere in Canada. Often 
a camp operator will be able to make 
his best deal locally. The soundest ad¬ 
vice I can offer once again is ask an 
expert and shop wisely. 


A PRAYER FOR LEADERS 

Lord of all learning and leaders, 

At best we blunder along 
While ours is the honour to forge 
out ahead, 

A daring and pioneer throng. 

Too easily sure and contented 
With successes of yesterdays, 

While Youth has the untried Tomorrow 
Calling to untrodden ways. 

May all of our short-comings shame us 
Till we learn to be humble and wise. 
Ready as seers and as prophets 
To lift up eager young eyes. 

5 Tis not our task to furnish the mind 
But to fan a flame in the soul, 
Sending them forth with a will and 
a dream 

To their high and potential goal. 

Give us, O Lord of all leaders 
A sense of our sacred task, 

The equipment needed to face it 
And a blessing, we humbly ask. 

—Mary S. Edgar

Church Service—Wabanaki Boys’ Camp—July 17, 1966 
Assemble silently (at flagpole area)—summoned by troubadour—Paul Abbott 
Song: “Lonesome Valley” (1st verse repeated) Paul Abbott 

Leader: “Christ loved to walk in the beautiful outdoor world which His Father 
had created. There He found peace and solitude to hear His Father’s voice 
and to talk with Him. There He often chose to teach so that those who 
listened would know by the beauty that God was real and wonderful. As a 
rabbi of Israel, He sought to teach His people.” “Let us, this morning, now 
walk in God’s great outdoors, and as we walk, let us think of those places 
where the Master walked. Let its imagine ourselves in another country, many 
miles away where He walked. Let us follow quietly: In His Steps!” 

(Group walks silently to back beach led by troubadour singing Lonesome 
Valley.) 

Assemble (on beach) 

Scripture: Matt. 3:13-17—Allan Kaufman 

Leader: “Christ was a man who knew how to be humble. Fie was not afraid to 
offer Himself for baptism—although as a man without sin He did not 
require it. John expressed surprise that He would come to be baptized. In 
fact He offered to exchange places. 

How often we feel that people in high places or in authority should not be 
asked to do menial tasks. How often people in those positions feel that they 
are too good or too important to be bothered by little things or to soil their 
hands. Camp has positions like these. Perhaps we should ask ourselves if we 
are hiding behind them. 

Do we as staff members use our positions for our own self-importance? 

Do we count more heavily on our authority or do we try to win respect by 
showing respect. As campers do we demand that staff members cater to us 
almost like servants? Are there jobs we think are beneath us? Who is 
willing to trade places with the kitchen or General Service staffs for a day 
and to clean up our garbage and the kybos?”

Canadian Camping 




by Bruno Morawetz, Ph.D. 


TIDBITS 

FROM THE CANADIAN CAMPING CONFERENCE 
Inn On The Park, Toronto, 1967 


Returning from his first medical con 
vention the fledgling physician was 
asked how he had enjoyed himself. “It 
was an excellent conference and, lei 
me add. the girls I met were really 
terrific”. As a successful middle aged 
practitioner his reply to the same ques¬ 
tion was: “It was a fine convention 
and the papers read were most inter¬ 
esting and stimulating”. Just before his 
retirement he attended his last con¬ 
vention and his report was: “It was 
a great gathering of eminent men and 
what is best of all (leaning over to the 
person’s ear) I had a bowel movement 
at the regular time each morning”. It 
took the dyspeptic Epicurus to make 
the pronouncement that a good diges¬ 
tion is one of life’s greatest goods. 

To Aid the Body and Soul 

There is nothing like a hearty belly 
laugh to case the digestion and to aid 
the soul. Those delegates who were 
fortunate to squeeze into the Trillium 
Room to hear “The Humorous Side of 
Camping” have had the all-too-rare 
experience of a sustained belly laugh. 
(No wonder the mountain of goodies 
disappeared so quickly at the Exhibi¬ 
tors’ Coffee Party which followed!) 
The Rev. David Hartiy, President of 
the Nova Scotia Camping Association, 
held his audience for nearly one hour 
with yarns of varying veracity: the 
nudist party at his church camp with 
the delicate pieces of clothing left by the 
fugitives at the appearance of his cleri¬ 
cal collar; the visit by the Bishop in the 
middle of a Japanese supper surprising 
the director with his pants up but a 
shirt bedecked with slimy spaghetti. 


Little did the late Pope John realize 
what he had done when he opened the 
“Window” to the world. He could not 
have forseen that priests of the church 
would encourage their flock to finger 
the knees of the lady next to them 
under the pretext of doing an action 
song! It is no wonder that dumb¬ 
founded latecomers dropped their jaws 
at the sight that greeted them: a 
densely filled room of semi-hysterical, 
tittering, bellowing, guffawing, writh¬ 
ing, doubled-over camp people. For 
the sake of his missionary plans and 
the African natives it is hoped that 
Ed Sullivan will not discover Rev. 
Hartiy before lie leaves. 

Packed with Substance 

After three full days of meetings, 
sessions, panels, workshops, “Spring¬ 
boards” and “Feedbacks” the delegates 
were entitled to some comic relief. All 
day Wednesday the CCA Board met 
in solemn assembly and that night its 
deliberations were consummated by the 
Annual Meeting. The free flowing 
“After Taps” session helped to unwind 
some of the keyed up members and to 
wind up the low key ones. 

By the afternoon of the next day the 
delegates were in a position to hear 
Dr. Hcdley Dimock’s keynote address 
on the Individual. From “Springboard 
No. 1” Dr. Dimock lectured to camp 
directors urging them to change from 
repressive to participative methods of 
programming. In the “Feedback” ses¬ 
sions the directors “participated” by 
getting back at him. 

page 99 please 


' Toronto, Canada, April 1967

A dele Ebbs 

President, Ontario Camping Association 


AMONG 

Adele Ebbs began her camping career 
as a verv young infant. She has con¬ 
tinued it ever since. Her mother and her 
father, the late Taylor Stattcn who was 
Director of the Y.M.C.A. camp on 
Lake Couchiching, took Adele to camp 
with them when she was a few weeks 
>ld. Hence the nickname, “Couchie”. 
The summer included a canoe trip: it 
is not recorded that Adele did any of 
the paddling, but for those who know 
her it does not seem impossible. 


During the following summers. Couchie was at cam]) wherever her father was 
Director. In 1921 he started Ahmek. a private camp for boys in Algonquin Park. 
Couchie was the only girl camper. In 1924 Taylor Statten opened a sister camp, 
Wapomeo, for girls. Rumour has it that bis primary purpose was to provide an 
appropriate camping environment for Couchie! Since then she has been at Camp 
Wapomeo as camper, counsellor, assistant director to her mother, and now as 
director. 


Couchie was a pioneer in canoe tripping. Her uncle, Wallace Forgie, took 
her on her first big canoe trip through Temagami when she was ten years old. 
Since then, she has canoed through almost all of Algonquin Park. In fact, in 
1926 she and a party of Wapomeo campers visited Glen Bernard outside the 
northwest boundary of the Park and paddled the long, difficult route back to 
Canoe Lake. This was probably the first inter-camp visit by canoe—at least for 
girls. Last summer she visited Quetico to see how a trip of her campers was 
faring. 

Couchie is a bit of a waterfowl. She loves and also excels in swimming, 
paddling, sailing, fishing and driving a variety of somewhat eccentric motor 
powered boats through the waterways of the Canoe Lake region. She also has 
deep interest in wildlife and nature and most of all in human beings who compose 
her staff and campers. 

Despite this continual career in camping, Mrs. Ebbs has had time for many 
other activities and interests. She attended Brown School and later the Bishop 
Strachan School where she was on hockey, lacrosse, basketball teams; she also

OURSELVES 


The Reverend David Hartry or 
“Father Dave” as he is affectionately 
called by the many campers who have 
come under his influence, lias been in 
the camping business one way or an¬ 
other for more than half of his 29 
years. He is. at present, the director 
of St. Anne’s Anglican Youth Camp in 
western Nova Scotia. 

Born in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Mr. Hartry received his early education in the 
Halifax City Schools. After high school he attended the Nova Scotia College of 
Art. Halifax, and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts, receiving his degree of 
Bachelor of Fine Arts and a Diploma in Art Education. 

Following graduation, and before he decided to enter the ministry, Mr. 
Hartry was employed with the Halifax Y.M.C.A. where he worked full-time 
with Hi-Y and Boys’ Clubs. Being very interested in youth work. Mr. Hartry 
also spent much time with the. young people in his home parish of the Cathedral 
Church of All Saints, Halifax, and with the youth in the camping field. 

After a year’s youth work, Mr. Hartry attended the University of King s 
College and, after graduating in Theology, was appointed to the parish of Round 
Hill. Annapolis County in western Nova Scotia. This same year. 1964, he married 
Janet Sinclair, also of Flalifax who is a school teacher and a former camp 
director. 

Mr. Hartry began his camping career at a tender age as a camper at Camp 
Sunshine, Halifax County. In his teen-age years he was a Counsellor In Training 
and Counsellor at Big Cove Camp (Halifax Y.M.C.A.) and later served for 
three years as Craft Director and Senior Staff' Member at the same camp. In 1961 
he directed his first camp in Griinshaw, Alberta, with the Missionary Department 
of the Anglican Church of Canada. The following year he was appointed the 
camp director of the Anglican Youth Camp. Halifax County, one of the largest 
camps in Nova Scotia. He held this position for three years and it was during 
this time that he was ordained Deacon in the Anglican Church of Canada. 

An active member of the Nova Scotia Camping Association, Mr. Hartry 
has held several executive positions. Fie has been Secretary, Editor of the

Canadian Camping 



by Madge K . Mitchele 


ARCHERY IN THE CAMP PROCRAM 


Fit the Programme to the Child— 
one of the first and most frequent words 
that come from a child’s mouth, when 
he has started to reason, is “Why”? 
And so, if we are concerned with the 
child’s, and the camp activity, let us 
say, Why — Archery? 

The answer to this question is amaz¬ 
ingly simple, and can be reduced to 
seven points: 

1. Archery is is one of the most ancient 
pursuits of man, from the standpoint 
of food and defence, and one of the 
most modem sports, from the stand¬ 
point of modem engineering design 
in equipment used. Therefore, for 
colour and romance and general in¬ 
terest, it appeals to children and 
adults alike. 

2. Archery is a truly healthful sport. 
It exercises finger, wrist, arm, shoul¬ 
der, chest, stomach and leg muscles 
to an amazing degree. It does for 
the archer what rowing used to do 
for the male fonn, takes inches off 
the waist line and puts them on the 
chest. Think of the advantage to the 
opposite sex when this marvelous 
transferrence occurs! 

3. Archery is a remarkably safe sport. 
The secret of this is that a bow 
cannot be “loaded” unknown to the 
archer. It is still just a piece of fiber¬ 
glass with a dacron bow-string until 
the arrow is drawn. With any in¬ 
telligence in Archery Range lay-out, 
its clear accident record should con¬ 
tinue indefinitely. 

4. Archery is a sport for all ages and 
both sexes. From the six year old to 
the sixty year old it can offer the 
same appeal. 


5. Archery can be competitive or non- 
competitive , according to the need of 
the camper and the programme. 

6. Archery is an extremely inexpensive 
sport from the standpoint of dollars 
spent to numbers participating. 

7. Archery takes a minimum of trained 
staff and a minimum of set-up. In 
keeping with the theme of the Con¬ 
ference, please note that the benefits 
of the sport to Campers were covered 
by the first five points, the benefits 
to the Camp Owners and Directors 
by the last two points. 

Qualifications 

Let us now say that we have made 
our point as to “Why Archery”? The 
next important angle is “How”? The 
single most important factor in the suc¬ 
cess of the Archery Programme is the 
“Instructor”. This person must not be 
the Councillor left over after every 
other sport and activity at camp has 
been taken care of. Good old “Bill” or 
“Mary” are conscientious and really 
like kids, but are not necessarily going 
to be able to make a howling success 
of the Archery Programme, since he or 
she will, most likely, string the bows 
inside out the first day and end up with 
a pretty sorry bunch of pseudo-archers. 
Archery Counsellors can make or break 
the archery programme, so they must 
know what they are doing. 

Over a period of twenty five years, 
no anxious archery “instructor-to-be” 
has contacted our firm without the offer 
of an afternoon or evening of instruc¬ 
tion and advice on equipment, teaching 
and planning of a summer’s instruc¬ 
tional programme. We wish to keep 
this offer open indefinitely. 


Toronto; Canada , April 1967 


91 



And what is the information we 

would pass on to the instructor to 

assure them of a successful summer? 

Some Guidance 

1. The location of the .Archery Range 
must be attractive. Too often the 
stubble field, away from water, trees 
and other human beings is alloted to 
archery, and instructor and group 
slowly bake from hour to hour, day 
to day, week to week, until, as in one 
camp, the Archery Range was known 
as “Sahara”. Even though the tar- 
gets are out in the open, for sake of 
safety of humans and equipment, the 
shooting line should be in the shade. 
A “Target-House” or equipment stor¬ 
age building at a close distance to the 
range is a must. The layout of stor¬ 
age within this shed is important for 
easy set up and storage. If the tackle 
must be carried some distance and 
the luncheon bell is about to go, the 
deterioration of the equipment is 
noticeable from day to day. 

2. The emphasis on Fun must ever be 
present. Correct care and use of the 
equipment is essential, and instruc¬ 
tion aimed at proficiency is essential 
also, but the fun factor must never be 
lost. If by the end of the summer 
the camper has caught the Archery- 
Bug, and wishes to go on with the 
sport it has been worthwhile. If a 
few campers have won proficiency 
badges, but many are bored or frus¬ 
trated, it certainly has not been a 
successful programme. 

3. The camper who is only mediocre in 
many activities may find his niche in 
archery. This is one sport where the 
protoype athlete is not necessarily the 
top archer, and this is good. There 
are groups of paraplegics shooting 
from wheel chairs, who are top 
archers; there are groups occupied 
in Physio-Therapy who become pro¬ 
ficient, but do not underestimate it 


as a sport. To shoot in National 
Competition for seven hours a day, 
for 5 or 6 days in a week cannot be 
attempted by the weakling. 

4. There are many pitfalls in planning 
an Archery Programme. The greatest 
pitfall for the Archery Programme is 
“Monotony”. Vary the type of shoot¬ 
ing from day to day, so that every¬ 
day has its own surprise: 

(a) novelty shoots — shooting at 
paper plates fastened to target, 
each plate with different score; 
have groups design novelty tar¬ 
get on sheets of paper in craft 
shop, leaf shoots, tree shoots, 
checker board shoots, etc. etc. 

(b) Field shoots, vary position, dis¬ 
tance, number of arrows, style of 
shooting, i.e. standing, sitting, 
kneeling, trick — (watch safety 
angle), etc. 

(c) Some sort of proficiency patch, 
tassle, crest, leather arrow heads, 
etc. if in keeping with camp 
philosophy. The next pitfall is 
allowing campers to shoot before 
good safety principles on shoot¬ 
ing and care of equipment have 
been taught. The third great 
pitfall is starting the classes at 
too great a distance from the 
target, so that they continuously 
miss, lose arrows and spend most 
of the period looking for them. 
Another great mistake often 
made is in not having a definite 
routine of “set-up” and “putting 
away” of equipment so that this 
chore does not all fall on the 
shoulders of one or two. A last 
and very common failing is to 
hope that the equipment, left 
over from one season will be 
quite adequate to start the next. 
If the bows are without strings, 
no arrows seem to match, many 
are without feathers, target faces 
for scoring are non-existent, the 
programme gets off to a miser- 


92 


Canadian Camping 



able start. Each of these details 
seem simple common sense, but 
can add up to many headaches 
over a period of two months. 

5. Choice of Equipment: 

(a) Target and Stand —For the sake 
of efficient scoring, life of arrows, 
safety and general appearance of 
the archery range, a regulation 
Marsh Grass or “Precision Pak” 
target should be used. These tar¬ 
gets are placed upon a tripod 
stand. The targets and stands can 
be removed and stored, against 
rain and thus their life will be 
vastly extended, and a saving in 
equipment costs effected. Baled 
straw or hay, when a well con¬ 
structed framework is used can 
prove feasible, but often becomes 
soft, allowing “pass-through” be¬ 
fore the end of the camping 
season. 

(b) Faces —purchase full size faces 
for your target size and also 
smaller ones for variety. 

(c) Backstops —A new Nylon Mesh 
Curtain known as Arrowmesh®, 
lias revolutionized indoor shoot¬ 
ing. Since Nylon is affected by 
Ultra-Violet rays, it will deter¬ 
iorate after some time in direct 
sun light. Some Directors feel 
that it is still a worthwhile ex¬ 
penditure as it saves arrows and 
eliminates time spent looking for 
lost arrows. 

(d) Bows —for Junior Archers—5 to 

10 years old, a fiberglas bow, 
straight limb, approximately 54" 
in length, pulling weight 15 to 
20 lbs., for Intermediate ages— 

11 to 15 years, a fiberglas bow, 
straight limb, approximately 60" 
long, pulling weight 20 to 30 lbs. 
is practical. For more serious 
shooting in a 16 year and over 
group a full length adult fiber¬ 
glas bow, approximately 64" in 


length, pulling weight 28 to 40 
lbs. is best. Recurved bows are 
attractive, but not necessary in 
a camp programme. The weight, 
or pull on the bow should be 
kept light. Good technique is 
developed only when the archer 
can control the bow. 

(e) Arrows —a Practice arrow, with 
plastic nock, target point, target 
size feathers and colour bands to 
distinguish the arrow when scor¬ 
ing is necessary. Arrows should 
be bought in 26" and 28" 
lengths. Broken arrows can be 
repaired and then you auto¬ 
matically have a supply of short 
arrows. Too short an arrow is 
dangerous, as the archer may 
“over draw” wedging the point 
behind the bow. When the string 
is released, the arrow breaks, and 
one piece flies backwards. 

(f) Armgnards, Gloves, Shooting 
Tabs, Bow Strings—It is only 
logical that there should be suf¬ 
ficient guards, gloves etc. to take 
care of the maximum number ot 
bows being used at one time. 
Additional accessories greatly 
speed the process of instructions. 
A bow is only useable when the 
correct length of bow string is on 
hand. There should be extra 
strings on hand at all times. 

(f) As a complete article could be 
written on Archery Tackle alone, 
it should be sufficient to say that 
extra points, nocks, feathers and 
jigs for applying of same, keep 
the equipment in good condition. 
Often the camper who seems to 
be disinterested in most activi¬ 
ties, can find his niche as curator 
and repairman for the Archery 
Equipment. 

Si .Teaching Tips: Start the “would be” 

archer with a chalk talk on equip¬ 
ment and its care. They must learn 


Toronto, Canada, April 1967 


93 



to string a bow before shooting it, 
know not to snap the string without 
an arrow on to absorb the energy. 
When all this initial instruction is 
passed on, then start the actual shoot¬ 
ing. More instructors spoil their 
whole summer’s work by starting the 
campers at too great a distance, than 
any other way. If necessary, stand 
the new archer at only 5 yards from 
the target, so that each arrow will 
find its mark. This is especially true 
if the correct use of a sight is taught. 
Gradually move the archer back. Psy¬ 
chologically, they are not “smart” if 
they hit the target, but awfully 


“poor” if they miss it. This will help 
them become good archers from the 
very beginning, and guards against 
frustration and loss of interest. Scor¬ 
ing should be practical, rather than 
shooting hundreds of arrows without 
knowing accurately if archers are im¬ 
proving or otherwise. 

Probably there are dozens of ques¬ 
tions that come to the mind of the 
reader. I hope he or she will feel free 
to write to me for further information 
or clarification of statements in this 
article. 


Mrs. R. John Milchele has been actively 
connected with the family business “Archery 
Craft Co. Ltd”, Toronto, for twetity-seven 
years and is at the present time the Sales 
Manager. She has held Ontario. Canadian 
and International Championship records for 
many years in “Target”, “Field”, “Clout” 
a nd “Flight”. Mrs. Mitchele has also been 
actively connected with Archery instructions in 
Camps , Recreation Centres and Universities. 


WHITE BIRCHES 
by Catherine Van Wagner, 1966 


Now, in October, leaves of shimmering 
gold 

against the blue of sky and lake 

Almost cry out, “These are our days 
of greatest beauty, in splendor 
dressed”. 

And yet, the winter birches, pale 
against the spruce, 
stand serene and pure on blue 
shadowed snowy hill, 

Their branches etched against the 
wintry sky, and on my memory 
until winter comes again. 

As April sun and showers free 
the prisoned pale green, 
tender leaves, 

I look with joy on Nature’s miracle 
once more. 


What can be lovelier than birches 
in the Spring? 

Vireos and robins nest 

mid full blown green of May 
and June. 

Summer sun and moonlight glint 
through the rustling leaves, 
dappling the creamy bark. 

With graceful bend and sway, 

they meet the stormy wind’s attack, 

Their pliant strength withstanding 
Nature’s harsher mood. 

Summer, Autumn, Winter, Spring, 
no matter when I look, 

My senses lift, my eyes fill with delight 
to see white birches stand in beauty.

Canadian Camping 


DRAMA 


in 


by Marni Jackson 

Camp 


Too often at camp, drama becomes 
a rainy-day activity, or a time-filler 
between sports, instead of the enjoy¬ 
able and really useful experience it 
can be. If drama is merely “something 
to keep them busy” between sailing 
and hikes, the person in charge could 
be guilty of any of the following mis¬ 
takes: underestimating the campers— 
children are enthusiastic actors if they 
arc interested in what they are doing, 
but to resurrect dismal skits from the 
1938 Campfire Book is an insult to 
their imagination; approaching the job 
unrealistically—this is what happens 
when a leader comes to camp with 
visions of staging Richard II. and is 
piqued when the director vetoes rented 
costumes, or the children don t do 
justice to the verse. A young person’s 
natural talent is best brought out in a 
simple play involving their own ex¬ 
periences. The result is pretty unex¬ 
citing by Broadway standards, but if 
the leader aims at flawless theatre, 
he’ll soon be as discouraged as 
the campers; restricting drama to the 
camp stage, or one “major production” 
—other opportunities for drama may 
be lost in frantic preparation for the 
end-of-season spectacular. 

Brought to Life 

For example, church service and 
morning watch can be brought to life 
by putting the message into a dialogue 
performed by campers. A lesson drama¬ 
tized is fun to do and watch, as well 
as instructive. And campfires need not 
be dominated by last year’s skits . . . 
draw on incidents in camp (which 


always assume catastrophic propor¬ 
tions), and make them material for 
songs or spoofs. The drawn-out, un¬ 
original one-liners that return summer 
after summer to haunt Skit-nights are 
not nearly as hilarious as campers pre¬ 
senting a fashion show featuring What 
the Well-Heeled Staff Member is 
Wearing. Or a gripping re-enactment 
of the night when Cabin Five was 
terrorized by three grizzlies (i.c. one 
raccoon). Often these skits deal with 
trivial incidents or temporary in-jokes, 
but campers become wonderful hams 
and natural actors, when they are pre¬ 
senting something they are familiar 
with, something unique to their time 
at camp and the experiences they 
shared there. 

A Few Examples 

These suggestions are all rather 
vague: perhaps a few examples from 
my first experience as “director” (em¬ 
ergency prompter, usher, set-painter 
and curtain-puller) would be more 
illustrative. In previous years, our 
camp had staged popular musicals. 
These were drastically simplified, of 
course, and everyone overlooked the 
fact that this year’s Sound of Music 
costumes were last year’s Oklahoma 
wardrobe, which were . . . etc. etc. 
Through the efforts of a particularly 
inspired stage manager, one year Mary 
Poppins floated up into the rec hall 
rafters, right on cue. However, I 
thought something original, about 
camp, would be less formidable to 
stage, and more suited to the actors. 


Toronto , Canada , Ajml 1967 


95 


The result was not exactly My Fair 
Lady: “The Diary of a Camper” (“A 
Funny Thng Happened on the Way 
to the Back Dock”) simply synopsized 
the adventures of a camper’s first sum¬ 
mer, moving from her reluctance to 
come at all, to (a little propaganda) 
her reluctance to leave. Her diary, sus¬ 
piciously human despite the cardboard 
jacket, fulfilled the function of nar¬ 
rator, as well as being the voice of 
conscience and confidant to its owner. 
The rest of the cast, all between nine 
and thirteen years old, gleefully as¬ 
sumed the roles of notorious staff mem¬ 
bers, the “senior kids”, and occasionally 
played themselves as they presented a 
cross-section of camp life to the new¬ 
comer. We took songs popular with 
the oast and changed the lyrics to suit 
the situations. It was a little depressing 
when the campers, with an amazing 
capacity for affectionate satire, im¬ 
proved upon my attempts, but I 
quickly learned that what I had writ¬ 
ten was only the starting point . . . be¬ 
cause the campers were acting out 
events they had seen or experienced, 
they elaborated, ad libbed with aban¬ 
don, and created something quite their 
own. Next time, I am simply going to 
suggest an idea and take dictation. 
The leader with a preconceived idea of 
what he wants, who refuses to let the 
campers determine the shape, under¬ 
rates the imagination of children and 
loses many valuable suggestions. 

This is not to imply that every re¬ 
hearsal is inspired improvisation. Leads 
frequently contract poison ivy, dis¬ 
appear on canoe trips, or the heroine 
refuses to go on without her gum. I 
soon became calculatingly practical: 
the long moving speech in Act II has 
the character absentmindedly riffling 
through a comic book ... in which his 
lines are taped, just in case. A scav¬ 
enger hunt of the camp produced all 
the costumes. Sets, which in previous 
summers had involved elaborate murals 


which lost their effect at any distance, 
were minimal (I reminded them it was 
Stratford’s policy . . .). There was one 
basic back-drop suggesting a general 
outdoors scene, and specific changes of 
location were accomplished by “tab¬ 
bing on” cabins, sailboats, and recog¬ 
nizable landmarks of the camp. These 
were separately painted and cut out, 
with tabs on the back; slits were made 
in the appropriate spots on the set, and 
by adding or subtracting them, the 
particular area for each scene was des¬ 
ignated. I wondered how to solve the 
indoors scenes, until I noticed that the 
back of the stage itself looked exactly 
like the inside of a cabin—we hung a 
lantern on a wire dropped from the 
rafters, added a few sleeping bags, and 
that was that. When we switched again 
to an outdoors scene, the original set 
was replaced. 

A Challenge 

Unless your camp has an unlimited 
budget, you’ll find the materials you 
must cope with more of a challenge 
than the fledgling actors. If you find 
the fighting a little limited, make up 
for it by being as sensational as pos¬ 
sible . . . black-outs never lose their 
effect, and having the cast begin a 
scene in complete darkness, with flash¬ 
lights or candles may be a theatrical 
cliche, but not for the campers. At 
one point in our play, I wanted a spot¬ 
light; a staff member obliged by shining 
the high-powered boat-light from the 
side of the audience! Our set, func¬ 
tional as I thought it was, accidentally 
provided the best moments of humour. 
Since it consisted of shelfpaper, pains¬ 
takingly scotch-taped together, we 
treated it gently. But, despite our 
efforts, it began to rip away from the 
suspending rope as we set up for the 
last scene. In a gesture of genuine 
dedication to the theatre, our out-trip 
director (who was in the wings quelling 
stage-fright and supervising props) 


96 


Canadian Camping 


teetered on a ledge and held up the 
set throughout the last scene . . . with 
only his fingers visible over the top. 
A floodlight placed behind the set for 
a special silhouette effect threatened 
every minute to scorch him, but the 
show went on. 

Moral—if you haven’t a sense of 
humor, cultivate one. I was pleasantly 
surprised to discover our camp owned 
a make-up kit, but when we came to 
use it, we found instructions on how 
to simulate wounds for first-aid tests, 
with all the grisly ingredients provided. 
However, make-up is only necessary in 
so far as it is a morale-booster. In lieu 
of this, the campers can fashion beards 
or wigs, if only from the kitchen mop 
or crepe paper. 

And if there are no drama facilities 
in camp? Pick a suitable spot outside, 
forget any attempt at realism, and 
make people into props. If it’s not 
quite clear who is a tree and who is 
a table, the campers can make signs— 
the comic effect of opening and closing 
a human door (labelled “door”) — 
makes up for whatever artistic stan¬ 
dards you may have to sacrifice. 

It is tempting to rely upon the 
“naturals”, who can do every part, and 
frequently want to. But the shy, 
tongue-tide chorus member is often the 
most dependable; to him, one line is 
as important as a soliloquy, and he at¬ 
tacks it like another Laurence Olivier, 
despite his cries of despair right up 
until curtain-time. I still remember 
forgettable lines such as “I wonder 
where she is?” delivered with intensity 
and perfect, pear-shaped vowels—the 
one big moment for some camper in 
the chorus. Even if it means chopping 
up speeches, distribute the lines 
throughout the cast, in order that no 
one is left out, or has too many lines 
to learn. Also (on the practical side 


again), I found that when I assigned 
even one line to a camper, the small 
responsibility improved his perform¬ 
ance throughout the whole play, if 
only to make him a more spirited 
crowd member. 

Not everyone has to be on stage. 
Children who want to be involved, but 
who don’t care to perform, become very 
serious about poster-making, ticket¬ 
selling, and set-painting if you empha¬ 
size how important all these things are 
to the production. You’ll end up with 
a backstage choked with unnecessary 
prop-assistants and prompters, but 
they’ll all have fun, and feel they have 
contributed. 

Some people may argue this has no 
place in camp life — after Little 
Theatre, there will be creative writing 
courses and sculpture classes, and who 
will be getting back to nature? But 
you only have to see a skit to realize 
what potential children and the camp 
environment hold for drama, and how 
much more attention it deserves. Not 
because there “should” be drama in 
camp, but because children make won¬ 
derful actors, and acting often does 
wonderful things for children. 

—• 


Marni Jackson is twenty years old, lives 
in Burlington and is in her third year 
Honours English Language and Literature 
at the University of Toronto. During her 
college days she has acted in campus pro¬ 
ductions and next year hopes to direct a 
play . For two summers , Miss Jackson studied 
drama at the Banff School of Fine Arts and 
hopes to apprentice in summer stock on the 
east coast this summer . She has been a 
regular or “visiting” member for five years 
at Camp Wabanaki on Georgian Bay.

Because of a joint venture and part¬ 
nership of six Winnipeg service clubs 
and the Y.M.C.A. of Greater Winni¬ 
peg, an exciting new camp programme 
is being developed. Ever since the late 
1930’s when the Rotary, Kiwanis, 
Lions, Kinsmen, Optimist and Cos¬ 
mopolitan Clubs and the Winnipeg 
Y.M.C.A. incorporated themselves to 
own and operate a resident boys’ camp, 
a friendly co-operative spirit has been 
generated in camping programmes for 
children. 

A Day Camp Project 

By 1962 the need for a resident 
camp for underprivileged boys had 
rapidly diminished. A number of local 
agencies who had referred boys began 
to develop camps of their own. The 
seven groups were faced with a prob¬ 
lem. They had a campsite called Camp 
Manitou that was conveniently located 
on a pleasantly wooded site, on the 
Assiniboine River, complete with dining- 
hall, cabins and a swimming pool and 
only foumteen miles from the center of 
Winnipeg but without a ready source 
of campers. For some months consider¬ 
ation was given to selling the site and 
liquidating the assets until a proposal 
was made to use the site as a day camp 
center. The Winnipeg Y.M.C.A. con¬ 
sisting of five branches each operating 
day camp programmes at different 


CAMP MANITOU 

by Doug McEwen, 

Director of Cam pins* 

Y.M.C.A. of Creater Winnipeg 
President, Canadian Camping Association 


centers, pressed for the opportunity. 
Permission was granted but some con¬ 
cern was expressed that a desire to 
provide camping opportunities for 
underprivileged children might be for¬ 
gotten. It was suggested that a study 
should be undertaken to examine other 
ways in which the camp might be used. 

In 1963 four branches of the 
Y.M.C.A. operated day camp pro¬ 
grammes making use of the site. Service 
clubs prov ided funds for the mainten¬ 
ance of facilities and the hiring of a 
“superintendent” of the camp to over¬ 
see its use and make sure that main¬ 
tenance functions were carried on. No 
rental fees were levied on these day 
camp groups and so their only costs 
were for programme, leadership and 
transportation. During that summer the 
number ol children who used the site 
jumped to 646 from 123 in 1961 when 
the camp had been used for resident 
camping. In addition, churches. Scouts 
and Guides, fraternal organizations and 
other Y.M.C.A. groups were invited to 
use the camp for camp-outs, weiner 
roasts and even winter camping during 
the prairie January period. Some 808 
persons responded in that first year and 
the number of persons has doubled 
since that time to a point where an 
estimated 1600 people used this former 
camp site for camping or outdoor ac¬ 
tivity in 1966. And that’s in addition to 
day camp programmes which now total 
over 7000 camper days! 

Another interesting fact emerged. In 
1960, during the life of resident camp¬ 
ing, camperships had been given to 79 
boys but in the years since the day 


98 


Canadian Camping 


camping programme began, there have 
always been more than 200 boys and 
girls assisted by means of cost subsidies 
to participate in a camping programme. 

In The Partnership 

The service clubs in the partnership 
did much more than simply provide 
funds to maintain the site. An extensive 
study was undertaken which resulted in 
two major recommendations. The first 
recommendation has been accepted and 
acted upon. This involved the develop¬ 
ment of the camp as a permanent day 
camp center adding facilities valued at 
$30,000. Each group involved in owner¬ 
ship including the Y.M.C.A., put up 
a share of the funds required. A second 
swimming pool for instructional pur¬ 
poses, a dock for canoeing and several 
buildings are now tangible evidence of 
this development. 


A second recommendation which sug¬ 
gests the development of a year-round 
conference center for youth, on the 
same property but not hampering its 
use as a camp site, is being considered 
and estimates of initial costs run to 
approximately $300,000. 

There is a uniqueness to all of this— 
not because a resident camp ceased to 
exist — that happens with unfortunate 
regularity. But because the development 
of a day camp park and conference 
center is a joint venture of a large 
number of business men who have not 
lost sight of the values of camping as 
a character devopment programme and 
who have, by their own resources, set 
out to meet the changing needs in 
camping with an enthusiasm which is 
an encouragement to us all.

he learns new skills (orienteering and 
crafts were all-day sessions) he starts 
to think about his work early and more 
than anything, he senses that he be¬ 
longs to the wide and growing fellow¬ 
ship of the finest young people of our 
aged country.

ter for its conferences. The Convention

A CAMP 

for Problem Campers 


by Skip Lumley 

Frontier Forest Camp provides diagnosis 
and treatment for emotionally disturbed boys. 


Frontier provides a service to the 
community of a kind distinct from the 
organized camping movement. The 
constituents of a camping experience, 
as a boy would understand them, are 
out-door activities and a peer group in 
which to mingle. On these, most boys 
can build substantially and achieve a 
greater degree of responsibility and 
independence. 

Camps provide the opportunities for 
using and enhancing physical and 
social skills, but their success is depend¬ 
ent on an adequate amount of sociability 
and physical adeptness as part of the 
camper’s original equipment. With a 
nonnal amount of direction and super¬ 
vision a normal boy will easily perfect 
his level of both skills. 

Without Skills 

Problem campers are boys who come 
to camp without these skills, or without 
enough of them. Also, they have needs 
which a camp can’t usually provide. 
Imagine twenty twelve year olds with 
an emotional level of two year olds set 
loose on your site. You can easily see 
that most camps are not designed for 
emotionally disturbed boys. 

At Frontier Forest Camp the setting, 
the games and the activities are only 
accessories to the functions of diagnosis 
and treatment of each boy’s unhealthy 
emotional life. The site and the pro¬ 
gramme are not provided primarily for 
the obvious reasons, but they serve to 
remove the camper from his home en¬ 
vironment and thus they provide an 
opportunity for close observation. 


The focus in Frontier’s programme 
is on what is often called the third 
dimension of camping—the interaction 
between camper and camper, and cam¬ 
per and staff. Such a situation is needed 
to study and to remedy a boy’s prob¬ 
lem and to construct a long range plan 
to help him. 

Location 

The camp is located on Bulpit Lake, 
one mile from Hermon, Ontario, along 
an almost impassable trail, fondly 
called the Frontier-Hermon Freeway. 
Hermon is about fifteen miles from 
Bancroft, north of the Kawartha Lakes 
District. 

With emotionally disturbed boys, 
complete isolation is important. For¬ 
tunately no one else lives on the lake. 

The boys are housed in five bell 
tents ranged along the north shore of 
the lake, with one overnight tent 
perched on the top of a nearby hill. 
The infirmary is on the opposite side, 
while the new lodge and craft house, 
as well as the Plaza Villa Red Shacks 
(staff quarters) occupy the east end. 

The camp owns a canoe and three 
rowboats, some bows and arrows, lots 
of rope, a pony and a mule and a dying 
five ton truck called “Supersquash” in 
which the boys go on truckatiours. 

Until 1966 Frontier operated two, 2 
week camps in August for twenty boys 
each and the staff-camper ratio has 
always been maintained at one to one. 

There are a few wistful wishes each 
year for more facilities and more camp 
periods, but it should be remembered 
that in the case of facilities, simplicity 
is the better part of treatment. The 
boys do not find the programme lack¬ 
ing, rather, they appreciate the lack 
of confusion and the absence of ex¬ 
citement provoking distractions. The 
one exception is the annual visit of 
the friendly farmer who brings his 
powerboat and water skiis. 


100 


Canadian Camping 



Life in the city brings to these boys 
a daily myriad of unstructured oppor¬ 
tunities, while at camp there are five 
highly structured programme areas— 
ponies, crafts, archery, swimming and 
watercrafts. This allows both boys and 
staff to see interpersonal issues more 
clearly and to deal with them more 
consistently. 

I remember one rather articulate 12 
year old telling me one morning, during 
a rare truce with adult world, “It’s 
kind of boring here”. When I asked 
him whether he liked being bored, he 
said, “Well ...” and smiled. I think 
he meant that he would rather be 
bored than continually anxious. And 
I don’t think he was really bored. 

Personnel 

For staff members a two-week session 
is a trying and tiring time. The boys 
are demanding, sometimes dangerous 
and always excrutiatingly frustrating in 
their open or disguised hostility toward 
adults. 

The boys were referred to camp by 
various institutions: Metro Toronto 
Juvenile Court, private and other agen¬ 
cies and through Glen Brubacker, a 
probation officer and the founder and 
part time director of Frontier. 

For the past five years, which covers 
the life span of the camp, one treat¬ 
ment agency has had a particularly 
close association with Frontier. It has 
supplied trained child care personnel, 
nearly a dozen campers and this clinic 
has done much of the preliminary 
screening. 

It should be pointed out that Fron¬ 
tier is embarking on a new format in 
1967. This will mean agency contacts 
on the board of directors level and a 
policy of drawing both staff and cam¬ 
pers from downtown Toronto churches. 

The boys I have worked with are 
tremendously challenging, their prob¬ 
lems range from violent aggression, 


through feminine identification to a 
behaviour of complete withdrawal. I 
consider it axiomatic that apart from 
such physical disorders as brain dam¬ 
age, all disturbed children come from 
openly chaotic or subtly destructive 
homes. In some backgrounds alcohol¬ 
ism, drug addiction or prostitution are 
present: in others material wealth and 
seemingly acceptable values have failed 
to protect the boys from their parents’ 
severe disturbances. They come to 
Frontier because they were born into 
this home and not into that one. 

Treatment 

The beginning and end of all treat¬ 
ment at Frontier has always revolved 
around two things: structure and con¬ 
trol. Structure appears in the afore¬ 
mentioned five, closely supervised ac¬ 
tivities. Each tent group attends two 
of these in rotation each morning. In 
the afternoons there are such group 
activities as games, hikes, truckathons 
and everyone, including the cook, goes 
along. Routines are, of course, the very 
essence of structure: morning wash, 
tent clean-up after breakfast, site im¬ 
provement, rest hour, just to mention 
a few. 

All camps use these features, but 
probably without emphasis on their 
therapeutic effects. At Frontier a boy 
must perform routines and behave ap¬ 
propriately. The concept of control is 
carried into practice by the absolute 
refusal of the staff member to accept 
any form of inappropriate behaviour. 
The hope is that the boy himself will 
feel secure enough also to reject it and 
to express his needs for attention and 
his desire for security in more accept¬ 
able ways. In short, if Freddy refuses 
to wash, Freddie can’t come to break¬ 
fast and should he appear he will be 
removed. His activity is broken off at 
the point at which he departs from 
what is expected of him. He may have 

page 105 please 


Toronto, Canada , April 1967 


101 


Your Library Shelf 

The postman has just delivered a 
parcel containing five attractive—and 
timely — paper backs, all related to 
camping. Although we’ve grouped 
them under “Your Library Shelf”, we 
might even more appropriately have 
said “For Your Pocket” because that’s 
just how compact they are both in size 
and content. 

“Canoeing for Beginners” by Ronald 
H. Perry, Price $1.10 was reviewed in 
the February issue of “Canadian 
Camping” but here are our observa¬ 
tions on the other four. 

“Good Times Around the Campfire” 
by LaRue A. Thurston begins by point¬ 
ing out that the programme around the 
camp fire is more than a recreational 
activity—it is a recreative, deeply en¬ 
riching experience. He then goes on to 
describe camp fire programmes suitable 
for every age of camper and all types 
of camps. In 128 pages and eight 
chapters you get some excellent leads 
for ceremonies, games, music, noisy 
games, stories all around the camp fire. 
Price $1.10 

Maybee because it is Centennial 
Year, it seems as if interest in our first 
Canadians has increasingly expanded. 
After all, our fellow Canadians, the 
Indians, were the very first campers 
in this country. “Indian Crafts for 
Campers” by Oscar E. Norbeck is en¬ 
hanced in interest by its numerous and 
excellent illustrations. This book de¬ 
scribes in condensed form the clothing 
and costumes, communication and 
record keeping, in fact the Indian’s 
whole way of life. And the author tells 
you how you can get your campers in¬ 
volved in such fascinating projects as 
making an Indian drum, moulding pot¬ 
tery, weaving, making Indian cooking 
gadgets for roasting, broiling and fry¬ 
ing—all this for just $1.10. 


Until recently most people thought 
of camping as purely a summer time 
experience. But more and more the 
fascination and feasibility of its winter 
time possibilities are emerging. That’s 
what “Fun in Winter Camping” by 
Harry D. Edgren and Gunner A. Peter¬ 
son is all about. And why not use your 
camp to its full potential ? The opening 
chapters provide practical advice on the 
kind of accommodation and clothing re¬ 
quired, the need for the leader to evalu¬ 
ate and prepare for certain hazards. 
Three chapters cover modes of trans¬ 
portation, winter sports, games, activi¬ 
ties, equipment. The final chapter 
indicates the kind of outdoor winter 
hobbies which will bring not only great 
pleasure but develop worth while skills 
and knowledge. Ho hum, why go south 
to the sun for a holiday? Why not 
north to sparkling snow and the stim¬ 
ulation of sharp, clear air. Price—you 
guessed it—$1.10. 

“Handbook of Trail and Wilderness 
Camping” by John A. Ledlie, deals, as 
the title indicates, with mobile camp¬ 
ing. It, too, is a down to earth, concise 
guide for anyone who is seriously think¬ 
ing about this increasingly popular kind 
of camping. With the Centennial Jour¬ 
ney absorbing our interest, we think 
this book might well have considerable 
appeal. True, some of us won’t be 
actively participating in this once in a 
lifetime experience but undoubtedly it 
will provide the stimulus for future 
treks of similar nature if of lesser 
dimensions. So, read about the kind of 
equipment you’ll need, the shelter you’ll 
require, the clothes you should have. 
Then, of course, there’s food and health 
and sanitation and emergency situa¬ 
tions. But why go on? For $1.10 you 
can get all the basic information you 
require and an urge—we think—to get 
trailing. 

All the above publications are avail¬ 
able from G. R. Welch Co. Ltd. y 222 
Evans AveToronto 18.

A Camp 

Director 9 s 
Diary 


One of our over-zealous kitchen boys 
shot a skunk at camp, and placed the 
perfumed body in the garbage bin. 
After breakfast Sue, age six, suggested 
to Mary, age seven: “Somebody should 


take it and throw it down the road 
somewhere”. Said Mary, the compas¬ 
sionate one: “Well, you wouldn’t like 
it if you were dead and somebody took 
you and threw you down the road 
somewhere, would you?” “Oh, yes I 
would,” replied Sue, “I’d want some¬ 
body to bury me . . . quick!”

rived”. Delegates from the other prov¬

PROBLEM CAMPERS 

to sit still until he is willing to comply. 
At that point he picks up where he left 
off. Obviously, this may involve a 
physical struggle, particularly during 
the first few days when every boy is 
testing to see if the staff really mean 
what they say. 

Unfortunately, structure and control 
are not enough for a boy’s long-term 
treatment programme. The camp’s 
wider function is to ascertain what else 
is necessary and to direct him to this. 
Consequently, each day, every staff 
member writes a log on the boys he has 
been involved with, which is usually 
the total number of twenty. These logs, 
together with the summary comments 
of the more highly trained observers on 
staff, are sent to the referring agent. 
It must be understood that not all staff 
are trained; if they were there might 
be an undesirable preponderance of 
brain power over “daily living power”. 

Boys from Frontier have gone out to 
protected classroom situations, residen¬ 
tial treatment centres, foster homes, 
some training schools and occasionally 
to hospitals. I am deeply impressed by 
Frontier’s role as an important com¬ 
munity service. 

A final word about the staff. More 
than anywhere else, at Frontier a staff 
member gets back each day what he 
gives to them. It begins with the very 
(yawn) early morning watches for staff 
only, and it runs through the whole 
day; when he is in need of help and 
out of the blue another appears at the 
critical moment; he senses this es¬ 
pecially in the nightly meetings at the 
Red Shack where everyone’s focus is 
on the individual child and information 
and mutual help bring a long day to a 
blissful end. It is a wonderful ex¬ 
perience to see a playing field with as 
many older persons -as boys and to feel 
yourself heavily involved with all of 
them. —•

Think of the campers as opportuni¬ 
ties, not as problems. Have continued 
respect for the campers as individuals. 
Don’t talk down to them. Always be 
on the lookout for the interests of your 
group. Be ready to guide or lead them 
whenever necessary. As often as pos¬ 
sible do what your campers do: Swim 
with them, play with them, make plans 
with them, hike with them, go to meals 
with them. Lead the evening prayers 
in your cabin. Talk over informally the 
happenings of the day. Be observant 
of and thankful for moments of beauty. 

Study your cabin group members as 
individuals. Discover the strong and 
weak points of your campers. Help 
them to overcome their weaknesses. 
Find out their interests, the things they 
can do well. Help each to develop some 
hobby, craft or ability as a means of 
hobby, craft or ability. 

If you cannot help the camper your¬ 
self refer him to the camp director. 
NEVER try to practice amateur psy¬ 
chiatry. All you can hope to do is to 
help each one to adjust to cabin life 
and give them a good time doing so. 
Ability to live with people is an im¬ 
portant objective in any camp ex¬ 
perience.

THEY DIDN’T DESCEND 
FROM US 

I hree monkeys sat in a cocoanut tree 

Discussing things as they are said 
to be, 

Said one to the others, “Now listen 
you two, 

I here’s a certain rumour that can’t 
be true, 

That man descended from our 
noble race”, 

1 he very idea is a disgrace. 

No monkey ever deserted his wife, 

Or starved her babies and ruined 
her life, 

And you’ve never known a 
mother monk 

To leave her babies with others 
to bunk, 

Or pass them on from one to another 

Till they scarcely know who is 
their mother. 

And another thing you’ll never see, 

A monk build a fence ’round a 
cocoanut tree, 

And let the cocoanuts go to waste, 

Forbidding all other monks a taste. 

Why, if I’d put a fence round a 
cocoanut tree, 

Starvation would force you to steal 
from me. 

Here’s another thing a monk 
won’t do— 

Go out at night and get on a stew, 

Or use a gun or club or knife, 

To take some other monkey’s life. 

Yes—man descended—the ornery 
cuss- 

But brother—he didn’t descend 
from us.

IT S A DATE 

Or rather it’s four dates—Monday. 
April 17th to Thursday, April 20th. 
We’re talking about the Canadian 
Restaurant Association Show to be held 
in tin* Automotive Building at the Can¬ 
adian National Exhibition Park. 

Fun, Fest *N Fare, the Centennial 
Year theme, has set the pace for this 
23rd annual event and more than 245 
companies will have exhibits. 

The programme sounds most com¬ 
prehensive and, although space does not 
permit elaboration here of the details, 
we think Camp Directors would find 
the Show well worth attending. It 
struck us that the display of menus 
from countries around the world might 
be of particular interest. This exhibit 
will include menus from all types of 
Canadian operations, those designed 
for Centennial Year and for other 
special occasions. 

Further information can be obtained 
from the Canadian Restaurant Associa¬ 
tion, 60 Avenue Road, Toronto 5, 
Telephone 923-8416.

BROCHURES OR LEADERS 


We’ve just been reading the Jan¬ 
uary 1967 issue of “Camping Magazine” 
the official publication of the American 
Camping Association. Under “Memo” 
from Ernie Schmidt to the A.C.A. mem¬ 
bership describing a long established 
and exceptionally fine camp he’d visited, 
Mr. Schmidt related this conversation. 
After a tour of the beautiful grounds and 
enthusiastic commendation of the ex¬ 
cellent facilities and equipment, he 
asked for a copy of the camp’s bro¬ 
chure. He was astounded to be told 
there wasn’t one. 

“But what do you show parents who 
want to send their children to your 
camp?”, enquired Mr. Schmidt. The 
director handed him a small booklet 
which listed only the names of the 
counsellors, their address and college, 
a statement of what each had accomp¬ 
lished and the records they held in 
their specialty. 

“That camp needs no brochure”, 
comments Mr. Schmidt, “the obvious 
quality of the staff speaks for itself.” 

With the increasing stress on the im¬ 
portance of leadership, many of us are 
asking, “What is a good counsellor?” 
Well, Ernie Schmidt says and most of 
you, we imagine, would endorse his 
definition: 

"The good counsellor has a sense of 
responsibility about his job as a leader; 
he can adapt himself to a changing 
situation; he is sensitive to people; he 
is able to communicate his ideas to 
others. The girls or the boys of the 
camp might say of their best coun¬ 
sellor, “he is fun” or “she is great”. 

And parents might well ask them¬ 
selves, “Is this young man or young 
woman good enough to handle my 
children?” 

“Would I want my children to pat¬ 
tern themselves after this young man 
or this young woman?” 

And to conclude — “Leadership is 
much better caught than taught”.
